name: Vanuatu
headline: Vanuatu is in Tier 1 (high concern) of the 28 August regional snapshot, with very high concern for drier-than-normal conditions over September–November 2026. A first-stage meteorological drought was declared on 21 July 2026 for all of Torba province and parts of Sanma, Penama and Malampa, and by mid-October SPC reported water scarcity in parts of the country. The national meteorological service expects the El Niño peak in November–January.

FAO/WFP/UN Women/WMO/OCHA historical susceptibility (eight El Niño + positive IOD events, 1982–2024): High on the drought side; Low–moderate on the wet side, 28 Aug 2026
SPREP El Niño advisory: among ~20 Pacific areas likely to see drought and below-normal rainfall, 12 Jun 2026
IFRC/Climate Centre briefing: drought very likely across Melanesia (PNG, Solomon Islands, Vanuatu, Fiji), Jun–Jul 2026
COSPPac (Pacific Meteorological Council): expected below-normal rainfall, Sep 2026
UNICEF EAPRO: drier conditions expected, with agricultural drought and water scarcity raising displacement and acute-malnutrition risk, 6 Oct 2026

hazard_outlook.text: Earth Sciences NZ (ICU #310) places Vanuatu in a significantly drier arc where many island groups have a high chance of being extremely dry (<25% of normal rainfall).

The FAO/WFP/UN Women/WMO/OCHA snapshot rates Vanuatu very high concern — drier; Earth Sciences NZ gives a large dry arc from western Micronesia and PNG to the Tuamotu Archipelago with a high chance of extremely dry conditions.
The Vanuatu Meteorology and Geo-Hazards Department expects the El Niño peak in this window (ABC News, 16 Sep 2026); the June regional snapshot placed Vanuatu's peak in Nov–Dec.

SPREP and COSPPac expect South Pacific cyclone genesis to shift eastward, away from Vanuatu, New Caledonia and the Coral Sea; CERF nonetheless sets prepositioning before November 2026 for its Vanuatu tropical-cyclone framework.

timeline.label: 20 May 2026
timeline.event: OCHA ROAP lists Vanuatu among dry-side countries of high priority for potential humanitarian challenges through December 2026.

timeline.label: 12 Jun 2026
timeline.event: SPREP El Niño advisory lists Vanuatu among ~20 Pacific areas likely to see drought and below-normal rainfall.

timeline.label: 13 Jun 2026
timeline.event: Over the 90 days to 13 June, seriously dry to extreme/exceptional drought conditions recorded in parts of northern Vanuatu.

timeline.label: 17 Jun 2026
timeline.event: June regional snapshot places Vanuatu in Tier 1 — highest concern, drier from August with peak in November–December.

timeline.label: By 6 Jul 2026
timeline.event: Vanuatu's meteorological service (VMGD) reports El Niño fully established; the Red Cross records Vanuatu as monitoring drought and rainfall extremes.

timeline.label: 11 Jul 2026
timeline.event: Over the 90 days to 11 July, extreme or exceptional drought (USDM) recorded in parts of northern Vanuatu.

timeline.label: 21 Jul 2026
timeline.event: Government declares the first stage of drought for all of Torba province and parts of Sanma, Penama and Malampa after three months of low rainfall.

timeline.label: 22 Jul 2026
timeline.event: VMHS classifies the declaration as a meteorological drought and warns that agricultural drought may follow if dry conditions persist.

timeline.label: 28 Aug 2026
timeline.event: Regional snapshot re-tiers Vanuatu as Tier 1 — high concern (convergence pathway), very high climate concern — drier for September–November.

timeline.label: 16 Sep 2026
timeline.event: Reported crop losses, rainwater dependence in northern islands including Santo, girls missing school to fetch water, and scabies and ringworm as rivers fall.

timeline.label: 6 Oct 2026
timeline.event: UNICEF names Vanuatu among countries expected to be drier, with agricultural drought and water scarcity raising displacement and acute-malnutrition risk.

timeline.label: 19 Oct 2026
timeline.event: SPC's regional summary reports water scarcity in parts of Vanuatu.

points: The 21 July drought declaration urged the population to conserve water for human and animal use; the meteorological service warned that months of regular rainfall would be needed to end the shortage (Anadolu Agency, 21 Jul 2026).
Northern islands including Santo face significantly below-average rainfall and rely on rainwater catchments (ABC News, 16 Sep 2026).
SPC reported water scarcity in parts of Vanuatu in mid-October (PINA/SPC, 19 Oct 2026).
A magnitude 7.3 earthquake affecting Santo disrupted water services for around 15,000 people in January–June 2026 (UNICEF EAPRO, 30 Jun 2026).
Up to 80% of the population relies on subsistence agriculture; vendors report island cabbage dying, poor banana fruit and rising fire risk to gardens (ABC News, 16 Sep 2026).

Farmers were asked to protect crops with stored water (Anadolu Agency, 21 Jul 2026); VMHS warned that agricultural drought may follow the meteorological drought if dry conditions persist (RNZ Pacific, 22 Jul 2026).
Scabies and ringworm are reported as rivers fall (ABC News, 16 Sep 2026).
Girls are missing school to fetch water and care for relatives (ABC News, 16 Sep 2026).
ActionAid Vanuatu fears rising violence against women blamed for food shortfalls (ABC News, 16 Sep 2026).
The Pacific carries a high GBV risk level, with critical gaps in GBV-in-emergencies and sexual and reproductive health in emergencies (GBV Coordination Asia Pacific / REGA, Q2 2026).
SPREP expected western Pacific states including Vanuatu to see reduced tuna access as the warm pool shifts east (SPREP, via APAC scorecard, 27 Jul 2026).
Higher ocean temperatures have directly increased fish mortality in Vanuatu, threatening subsistence fishers (OCHA ROAP, 20 May 2026).

Marine heatwaves of strong, severe or extreme intensity affected the western South Pacific between New Zealand, New Caledonia and Vanuatu in 2025 (WMO, State of the Climate in the South-West Pacific 2025).

Declared the first stage of drought on 21 July 2026 for Torba and parts of Sanma, Penama and Malampa, with water-conservation and crop-protection advice (Anadolu Agency, 21 Jul 2026; RNZ Pacific, 22 Jul 2026).
Government agencies meet weekly with the water and tourism sectors (ABC News, 16 Sep 2026).
ActionAid Vanuatu runs a women's network carrying official warnings "from one kitchen to the next kitchen" where there is no reception (ABC News, 16 Sep 2026).
The Red Cross was monitoring drought and rainfall extremes affecting water security and food production in Vanuatu as of 6 July 2026 (IFRC, 6 Jul 2026).

UNICEF is implementing and refining a subnational Children's Climate Risk Index and Disaster Risk Model in Vanuatu, and a grassroots preparedness initiative will support 10 to 15 local organisations in the country (UNICEF EAPRO, 30 Jun 2026).

Vanuatu's CERF anticipatory action framework covers tropical cyclones (US$1,500,000, under development); CERF's Pacific action window is prepositioning before November 2026 (OCHA/CERF secretariat, 30 Jun 2026).
No drought framework exists in CERF's Asia-Pacific El Niño-relevant set, which covers only Fiji, the Philippines and Vanuatu, all for cyclones (OCHA/CERF secretariat, 30 Jun 2026).

ADB stood ready to use its Rapid Resource Reprogramming and Deployment Option (3RDO) for Vanuatu, which the government wanted for the immediate fuel crisis and as a standing contingency mechanism (ADB, 12 Jun 2026).

history: 2023/24: subsistence farmers in Papua New Guinea and Vanuatu faced severe food shortages as drought destroyed staple crops such as sweet potato and taro (OCHA ROAP, 20 May 2026).
2023–2024: the Red Cross Red Crescent ran an Emergency Appeal for a cyclone in Vanuatu during the 2023–24 El Niño season (IFRC Asia Pacific, lessons from DREF and Emergency Appeal operations).

Across eight El Niño events paired with positive IODs (1982/83 to 2023/24), Vanuatu ranks High for below-average rainfall and Low–moderate for above-average rainfall; this is a pattern analysis, not attribution (FAO/WFP/UN Women/WMO/OCHA, 28 Aug 2026).

In a past powerful El Niño (event year not stated in the source), Vanuatu was among Pacific countries seeing worsening drought, with as many as 4.7 million people across the Pacific facing hunger, poverty and disease (Oxfam).
cautions: Agency rankings differ: the 28 August snapshot places Vanuatu in Tier 1, while the IASC ENSO Cell places it in its monitoring tier, because the Cell weights existing caseloads and fragility rather than the projected climate signal.

Cyclone signals point in different directions: SPREP and COSPPac expect South Pacific cyclone genesis to shift east away from Vanuatu, while CERF notes that El Niño combined with a positive Interdecadal Pacific Oscillation is typically associated with increased tropical-cyclone activity for its South Pacific frameworks, including Vanuatu's.

Fisheries readings differ: SPREP expected reduced tuna access for Vanuatu, but SPC's observed October list of western Pacific states with declining purse-seine catches names PNG, the Solomon Islands and FSM, not Vanuatu; the wiki treats SPC's as the observed reading.

Short rain events inside a broadly dry El Niño pattern can be misread as an end to drought; SPREP flags media misinterpretation, and Vanuatu's met service anticipates people asking, 'We're having rain, what El Niño is this?'
The Pacific EAR Watch rainfall product cited for the August–October outlook is an inter-agency met-service product marked not for public redistribution.
